prework: Complete the critical appraisal checklist for your article, with one or two notes per question.
Write a one-sentence BLUF: what you would do differently, or the same, because of this evidence.

checklist.heading: Are the results valid?
checklist.subtitle: Internal validity
items: Who was blinded (patients, clinicians, outcome assessors)?
Were baseline characteristics similar between groups?
Were crossovers or missing data substantial enough to affect the results?

checklist.heading: What were the results?
checklist.subtitle: Magnitude and precision
items: What were the effect sizes (HR, OR, RR, ARR, NNT, or NNH)?
What were the confidence intervals, and do they include a difference you would act on?
Were the results clinically meaningful, or only statistically significant?
Were harms or adverse effects reported?
Were there time-course patterns, such as an early difference that later closed?

checklist.heading: Will these results help my patients?
checklist.subtitle: Applicability
items: Does the study population match my patients (age, comorbidities, setting)?
Are the outcomes patient-centered (survival, function, pain, satisfaction)?
Are there practical barriers here (staffing, resources, protocols)?
How might local pathways differ from the study?

sessions.topic: TAP block for abdominal surgery: laparoscopic cholecystectomy and major abdominal procedures
sessions.purpose: This session sets a meta-analysis of TAP block versus wound infiltration for laparoscopic cholecystectomy next to a three-arm trial of liposomal bupivacaine, plain bupivacaine, and saline for single-shot TAP blocks before major abdominal surgery. The two papers ask different questions.
objectives: Separate a review of one operation and one comparator from a three-arm trial in a mixed surgical population.
Read pain and opioid results with their confidence intervals, not only the p-value.
Decide whether either paper should change routine use of a single-shot TAP block.

articles.label: Grape 2021, J Clin Anesth
articles.citation: Grape S, Kirkham KR, Akiki L, Albrecht E. Transversus abdominis plane block versus local anesthetic wound infiltration for optimal analgesia after laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis. J Clin Anesth. 2021;75:110450.

articles.label: Turan 2026, Anesthesiology
articles.citation: Turan A, Ali Sakr Esa W, Brooker J, et al.; for the CLEVELAND Trial Group. Liposomal bupivacaine, plain bupivacaine, and saline for transversus abdominis plane blocks: the CLEVELAND randomized trial. Anesthesiology. 2026;144(3):546-558.

pico.population: Adults in trials of TAP block versus wound infiltration for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
pico.outcomes: Pain at rest, later pain scores, opioid use, nausea and vomiting

pico.population: Adults having major open or laparoscopic abdominal surgery
pico.intervention: Bilateral four-quadrant TAP block with liposomal bupivacaine, or the same block with plain bupivacaine
pico.comparison: Bilateral four-quadrant TAP block with saline

left.title: Grape 2021 — laparoscopic cholecystectomy
points: The review compares TAP block with wound infiltration, not with placebo.
Across the included trials, pain and opioid use favored the TAP block for this operation.
left.conclusion: For laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the review finds TAP block the stronger of these two local-anesthetic techniques.

right.title: CLEVELAND 2026 — mixed major abdominal surgery
points: Single-shot four-quadrant TAP blocks were placed before incision.
Liposomal bupivacaine, plain bupivacaine, and saline led to similar opioid use and pain scores through 72 hours.
right.conclusion: In this mixed open and laparoscopic population, a routine preincision TAP block did not separate from saline.

bottomLine.takeaway: A result that favors TAP block over wound infiltration for laparoscopic cholecystectomy does not, by itself, justify routine single-shot TAP blocks before major abdominal surgery.

sessions.topic: EEG-targeted anesthesia and postoperative delirium in older adults
sessions.purpose: Review of evidence from the ENGAGES trial and the BALANCED delirium study on the relationship between EEG-targeted anesthesia and postoperative delirium.
objectives: Compare a depth-target trial (BIS 50 versus BIS 35) with an EEG-guidance trial (ENGAGES versus usual care).
Judge the size of any difference in postoperative delirium, not only whether a p-value crossed 0.05.
Decide where either result should change care of older adults having major surgery.

articles.label: Evered 2021, Br J Anaesth
articles.citation: Evered LA, Chan MTV, Han R, et al. Anaesthetic depth and delirium after major surgery: a randomised clinical trial. Br J Anaesth. 2021;127(5):704-712.

articles.label: Wildes 2019, JAMA
articles.citation: Wildes TS, Mickle AM, Ben Abdallah A, et al.; for the ENGAGES Research Group. Effect of electroencephalography-guided anesthetic administration on postoperative delirium among older adults undergoing major surgery: the ENGAGES randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2019;321(5):473-483.

pico.population: Adults 60 and older, ASA III–IV, having major noncardiac surgery expected to last at least 2 hours
pico.intervention: Volatile general anesthesia targeted to BIS 50
pico.comparison: Volatile general anesthesia targeted to BIS 35
pico.outcomes: Postoperative delirium; cognitive screening, mortality, length of stay, ICU admission
pico.time: Delirium during the stay; cognition at discharge, 30 days, and 1 year

pico.population: Adults 60 and older having major surgery under general anesthesia at a US academic center
pico.intervention: EEG-guided anesthesia aimed at limiting EEG suppression and excessive depth
pico.comparison: Usual anesthetic care, without a mandated EEG target
pico.outcomes: Postoperative delirium; EEG suppression, anesthetic dose, hypotension, awareness, complications
pico.time: Delirium on postoperative days 1–5; other outcomes through the stay and 30 days

sections.heading: Are the results valid?
notes: Randomization was computer-generated and allocation was concealed. Patients and outcome assessors were blinded. The anesthesia clinician was not.
Baseline age, comorbidities, cognition, and surgical type and duration were similar.
Analysis was intention-to-treat, with little crossover or missing delirium data.
The comparison is a BIS target of 50 versus a BIS target of 35. It is not usual care without a BIS target.

sections.heading: What were the results?
notes: Delirium on postoperative days 1–5 was 19% with a BIS target of 50 and 28% with a BIS target of 35.
The pre-session handout calls that reduction modest and statistically significant, and it records no increase in awareness.

sections.heading: Will these results help my patients?
notes: The trial enrolled adults about 60 and older having major noncardiac surgery.

sections.heading: Are the results valid?
notes: Randomization was centralized and allocation was concealed. Patients and delirium assessors were blinded. The anesthesia clinician was not.
Baseline age, frailty, cognition, and surgical and anesthetic characteristics were similar.

The analysis was a modified intention-to-treat of randomized patients who had surgery. Some EEG targets were not met. Missing delirium assessments were balanced, and the handout notes that sensitivity analyses stayed consistent.

sections.heading: What were the results?
notes: Delirium was 26% with EEG guidance and 23% with usual care.
The handout treats that gap as neither statistically nor clinically meaningful, and it records no increase in intraoperative awareness.

sections.heading: Will these results help my patients?
notes: The trial enrolled adults 60 and older having major surgery, mostly noncardiac, in a US academic practice.
The population is broad and pragmatic.

reminders: A lighter BIS target reduced delirium modestly when BIS 50 was compared with BIS 35.
EEG-guided anesthesia, compared with usual care, did not meaningfully reduce delirium in ENGAGES.
Delirium prevention takes more than an anesthetic-depth target.

sessions.topic: Spinal versus general anesthesia for hip fracture, set against elective total hip arthroplasty
sessions.purpose: This session uses the REGAIN trials of spinal versus general anesthesia in older adults having hip-fracture surgery, and sets those findings against best-practice recommendations for elective total hip arthroplasty.
objectives: Practice critical appraisal with a structured checklist: validity, results, and applicability.
Interpret effect sizes and confidence intervals, rather than stopping at the p-value.
Apply the findings to clinical vignettes in anesthesia practice.
Recognize the limits of generalizing fracture-trial data to elective total hip arthroplasty, where ERAS pathways and regional techniques are standard.

articles.label: Vail 2024, Anesthesiology
articles.citation: Vail EA, Feng R, Sieber F, et al.; for the REGAIN Investigators. Long-term outcomes with spinal versus general anesthesia for hip fracture surgery: a randomized trial. Anesthesiology. 2024;140(3):375-386.

articles.label: Ritz 2022, Ann Intern Med
articles.citation: Ritz J, Memtsoudis SG, Sieber F, et al.; for the REGAIN Investigators. Pain, analgesic use, and patient satisfaction with spinal versus general anesthesia for hip fracture surgery: a randomized clinical trial. Ann Intern Med. 2022;175(7):952-960.

articles.label: Haslam 2024, BJA Education
articles.citation: Haslam N, Halvey E, Scott C. Perioperative care of patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty. BJA Educ. 2024;24(6):183-190.

pico.population: Hip fracture, age 50 and older, ambulatory before the fracture

pico.outcomes: Pain, prescription analgesic use at day 60, satisfaction

pico.intervention: Neuraxial anesthesia, or regional anesthesia and local infiltration, inside an ERAS pathway
pico.outcomes: Complications, mobilization, length of stay, pain control

cases: An elderly fracture patient on anticoagulation.
A hip-fracture patient with severe coronary artery disease.
An elective total-hip patient on an ERAS pathway.

left.title: Hip fracture surgery
points: No difference in 1-year survival or the ability to walk between spinal and general anesthesia.
Spinal anesthesia was associated with more pain on the first postoperative day and higher prescription analgesic use at day 60.
left.conclusion: For hip-fracture surgery in older adults, the two anesthetic types led to similar major long-term outcomes in these trials.

right.title: Elective hip replacement
points: Neuraxial anesthesia, or motor-sparing regional anesthesia with local infiltration, sits inside an ERAS pathway.
General anesthesia alone is not treated as best practice for a planned replacement.
right.conclusion: For planned hip replacement, neuraxial or regional technique remains the practice this session treats as standard.

bottomLine.takeaway: Hip fracture is not elective total hip arthroplasty. Findings from the fracture trials should not be carried over to planned replacement without looking at the pathway the patient is actually on.
